name: Radionic frequency devices

lead: Radionic devices are boxes of dials, wires and knobs that practitioners say can detect and rebalance an individual's body 'frequencies'. In appearance-minded circles they are mentioned as a way people hope to improve skin, weight or general vitality without products or procedures.

The approach goes back to physician Albert Abrams in the 1910s. Reviews of electromagnetic-therapy devices and reviews cited on Wikipedia describe no verified mechanism and results no better than placebo.

paras: Practitioners typically take a sample or a name, set a rate on the dials and 'treat' remotely or at a clinic; modern versions include software and handheld frequency units. Sessions are usually repeated over weeks.
The main documented concern is delay of effective care for real conditions. The FDA does not recognise a legitimate medical use for radionic devices, and some devices have been recalled.

chain: Practitioner dials a 'frequency' for a condition
Device is said to rebalance body energy
Claimed gains in skin, weight or vitality
angle.text: Users and practitioners say that rebalancing frequencies could improve skin, weight and energy, and so appearance. This is a claimed route; the proposed mechanism has not been verified.

lead: Radionic frequency devices are instruments, usually boxes with dials and electrodes or plates, that practitioners say can measure and adjust a person's energetic 'frequencies' to promote health. People who use them for looks hope to improve skin condition, body weight or general vitality by correcting what they believe are imbalances.[1]

The idea originated with American physician Albert Abrams, whose 1916 book launched his 'Electronic Reactions of Abrams' and who leased thirteen devices to practitioners.[1] The American Medical Association called him the 'dean of gadget quacks', and a 1924 Scientific American investigation concluded his method was an illusion.[1]
Reviews cited in the encyclopedia record that radionics has been found no more effective than placebo, and the FDA recognises no medical use for the devices.[1]

paras: Abrams claimed to detect disease by testing a blood sample on filter paper wired to a 'dynamizer' and to a healthy volunteer, and said he could treat by broadcasting matching vibrations.[1] Wikipedia notes that a radionic device may not form a working electrical circuit, and modern practitioners describe it as a focusing aid for dowsing.[1]

Abrams published Spinal Therapeutics (1909) and Spondylotherapy (1910) before his 1916 book, and became wealthy by leasing the devices.[1] Ruth Drown is listed among later notable practitioners.[1] In 2008 the VIBE machine received a Class I recall, completed in 2012.[1]

Scientists cited in the article say radionic claims conflict with accepted physics and biology and that no verifiable mechanism has been proposed.[1] Systematic reviews found radionics no more effective than placebo.[1]
No studies found. Reviews of electromagnetic therapy devices for conditions such as osteoarthritis, fracture healing and ulcers are a different category and are summarised on the Radionics page.[1]

timeline.event: New Concepts in Diagnosis and Treatment launches his electronic reactions method.[1]
Scientific American investigation finds the method an illusion.[1]
Class I recall of the VIBE machine.[1]
